OSTEOMYELITIS
NURSING PROCESS & 
COLLABORATIVE CARE
Group 13A: Sophia Bok, Destiny Eusebio, Sophie Goodgion, 
Ranita Menezes, Flor Navarrete, Robert Tiwari, and Jeffrey 
Yom
(Shah, 2020)

WHAT IS OSTEOMYELITIS?
• Infection of the bone 
• Classifications:
⚬ Hematogenous: caused by bloodborne spread of infection
⚬ Contiguous-focus: caused by contamination from bone surgery, open fracture, or 
traumatic injury
⚬ Osteomyelitis with vascular insufficiency: most common in patients with diabetes and 
peripheral vascular disease. Most commonly affecting the feet.
• Cauastive agents: more than 50% caused by Staphylococcus aureus or MRSA. Other pathogens 
include Streptococcus, Enterococcus, as well as Pseudomonas.
• Pathophyisology
1. Initial response to infection is inflammation, increased vascularity, and edema.
2.Thrombosis of local blood vessels typically occurs 2-3 days later, resulting in ischemia 
and necrosis.
3. Infection extends into medullary cavity and under the periosteum. If infective process is 
not treated, a bone abcess forms.
4.Sequestrum: dead bone tissue contained in the abscess cavity; does not easily liquify 
and drain.
5.Involucrum: new bone growth that forms and surrounds the sequestrum. (“Osteomyelitis”, 2026)

RISK FACTORS & PREVENTION
Risk factors
• Infections after untreated cellulitis, orthopedic surgery, open fractures, 
traumatic injuries, and reusable surgical site ink markers.
• Older adults, malnutrition or poor nutritional status, and obesity
• Patients with chronic conditions: diabetes, peripheral vascular disease 
(PVD), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and impaired immune systems
• Long-term corticosteroid therapy, immunosuppressive agents, and illicit 
IV drug use
Prevention
• Postpone elective orthopedic surgery if an active infection exists
• Administer prophylactic antibiotics at surgery and continue for 24 hours 
postoperatively
• Use hair clippers instead of razors/shaving in the operative region
• Use single-patient surgical site markers
• Remove urinary catheters and surgical drains ASAP
• Promptly treat soft tissue infections to prevent extension to bone
• Strict aseptic technique for postoperative wound care

EARLY DETECTION & HEALTH PROMOTION 
Nutritional & Health Support
• High-protein diet and vitamins to promote wound 
and bone healing
• Adequate hydration
• Glycemic & Chronic Disease control
• Lifestyle risk reduction
⚬ Smoking cessation
⚬ Weight management
⚬ Stress reduction
Local Cues
• Note bone discomfort
⚬ Constant, pulsating localized bone pain that intensifies 
with movement
• Perform frequent checks on the skin, prior surgical scars, 
and sinus tracts
⚬ Look for localized edema, erythema, warmth, and 
marked tenderness
• Daily foot self-exam
⚬ Nonhealing diabetic foot ulcers larger than 2cm in 
diameter
Systemic Cues
• Monitor body temperature at home
⚬ Sudden onset of chills, high fever, tachycardia, and 
general malaise
⚬ Low-grade afternoon/evening temperature spikes in 
chronic cases
• Pay attention to subtle early changes in physical functions
⚬ Altered gait, limping, or favoring one leg to avoid 
bone/joint pain

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
PAIN & TENDERNESS
• Localized bone pain and extreme 
tenderness may occur.
• Pain can be constant and pulsating 
and may become worse with 
movement.
SWELLING & W ARMTH
• The area over the infected bone may 
become swollen, warm, and tender 
due to inflammation.
FEVER & FATIGUE
• Acute osteomyelitis may cause 
fever, chills, rapid pulse, malaise, 
and generalized weakness as the 
body responds to infection.
• Low-grade fever may occur in 
chronic cases.
WOUND DRAINAGE
• Chronic osteomyelitis may present 
with a nonhealing ulcer or sinus 
tract that intermittently drains 
purulent material. 
(Jia et al., 2024)

DIAGNOSTIC TESTS 
& NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES
DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
• Blood tests: Acute osteomyelitis may show increased WBC and elevated ESR. In chronic osteomyelitis, WBC and ESR may remain normal. 
Anemia may be present in chronic cases.
• Blood & wound cultures: Used to help identify the organism causing the infection, although cultures may not always be positive.
• Blood cultures: Use aseptic technique and fill the aerobic bottle first, followed by the anaerobic bottle, when using a butterfly set. Label both 
bottles correctly and send them to the lab promptly.  
• X-ray: Early findings may show soft-tissue swelling. Bone changes such as periosteal elevation and bone necrosis may appear after 2–3 
weeks. 
• MRI / Radioisotope bone scan: help detect early bone infection and identify areas of involvement. 
• Bone aspiration: Bone specimens can help identify the causative organism and guide antibiotic therapy.
NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES
• Blood tests/cultures: Collect and label specimens correctly using aseptic technique and monitor WBC and ESR trends. 
• Cultures: Obtain blood, wound, or bone cultures before antibiotic therapy when possible to improve identification of the organism. 
• X-ray: Explain the procedure and assist with safe positioning while protecting the painful or affected extremity. 
• MRI: Screen for metal implants or implanted devices, remove metallic objects, and assess for claustrophobia. 
• Bone scan: Explain the procedure and encourage fluids afterward when appropriate to help eliminate the radioactive tracer. 
• Bone aspiration: Prepare the patient for the procedure and monitor the site afterward for pain, bleeding, drainage, or signs of infection.

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
General supportive measures
• Hydration, diet high in vitamins and protein, and 
correction of anemia
Immobilization
• The affected area is immobilized to decrease 
discomfort and prevent pathologic fracture of 
the weakened bone
Pharmacologic Therapy
• Bone infections require longer antibiotic use due 
to being mostly avasular
• Antibiotic therapy lasts from 6 to 12 weeks
Surgical Management
• Debridement
⚬ Indicated for chronic infection that does not respond to 
antibiotic therapy
⚬ Infected bone is surgically exposed, the purulent and necrotic 
material is removed, and the area is irrigated with sterile saline 
solution
• Wound Closure and Healing
⚬ The wound is closed tightly or packed and closed later through 
granulation or grafting
⚬ Cancellous bone grafts stimulate healing, large defects may 
require vascularized bone transfers or muscle flaps to improve 
blood supply, healing, and eradication of infection
• Bone stabilization
⚬ Internal fixation or external supportive devices may be needed 
to prevent pathologic fractures because débridement weakens 
the bone
** These procedures may be staged over time to ensure healing
Goal: To control and halt the infective process

MEDICATION MANAGEMENT & 
NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES
Antibiotic Therapy
• Long course (typically 6-12 weeks); often IV at first
⚬ Bone infections are harder to get rid of than soft tissue infections because 
bone is avascular  decreased penetration by medications→
• May switch to oral once the infection appears controlled
• Bone biopsy (Cx) before therapy to avoid false-negatives
• Empiric broad-spectrum therapy
⚬ Focuses on targeting the most likely pathogen [Gram-positive (Staphylococcus 
aureus->MRSA) and Gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas)]
￭ Standard combination: Vancomycin IV (to cover Gram-positive/MRSA) and  
Zosyn IV (to cover Gram-negative and anaerobes)
• There are many alternatives. For example, use cefepime instead of 
Zosyn if the patient has a penicillin allergy; it also has a lower AKI risk
• May be initiated before the organism is identified/while the culture is pending, then 
adjusted according to results
￭ Fluoroquinolones, like Ciprofloxacin, are good step-down agents; have 
excellent bone penetration and oral bioavailability
￭ Rifampin is prescribed for patients with hardware/implant infections
• Penetrates bacterial biofilms
• Must be used in conjunction with another antibiotic
• Check allergies before administering medications
• For vancomycin, infuse slowly to prevent infusion reaction (flushing)
⚬ Glycopeptides are nephrotoxic  important to monitor drug levels, BUN/Cr, →
and urine output
• Monitor the patient’s response to antibiotic therapy
⚬ VS, lab trends (WBC, ESR, CRP), appearance, pain score
• Assess the IV site for phlebitis, infection, or infiltration
• Report new warm, painful sites or sudden fever
• Watch for superinfection: oral or vaginal candidiasis, loose or foul-smelling 
stools
• Administer prescribed analgesics for pain along with nonpharmacologic measures
⚬ Acetaminophen, NSAIDS, opioids
⚬ Splinting, elevation, and gentle handling
• Patient education and adherence: teach medication name, dose, frequency, 
adverse effects; complete full antibiotic course, even after symptoms improve
Nursing Responsibilities

MEDICATION MANAGEMENT & 
NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES (CONT.)
Diabetic Foot Osteomyelitis
• Spreads from a foot ulcer into adjacent bone
⚬ Important considerations
￭ Becomes a polymicrobial infection (main difference): Gram-positives, Gram-negatives, and sometimes anaerobes all together
￭ Less antibiotic reaches the infection because of reduced blood flow
￭ Neuropathy results in less pain felt by patient  often presents late→
￭ Hyperglycemia impairs wound healing
Diabetic-specific management, treatment & considerations
• Glycemic control; target: 140-180 mg/dL
⚬ Insulin is often needed because infection raises blood glucose
￭ As infection clears, insulin dosage needs to be adjusted to prevent hypoglycemia
⚬ Hold metformin due to risk of lactic acidosis and acute kidney injury
• Fluoroquinolones can cause hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia
• Neurovascular and frequent wound checks are very important
⚬ Pulses, color, temperature, capillary refill, sterile dressing technique
• Renal dose adjustments based on GFR and creatinine clearance 
⚬ Prevents nephrotoxicity in patients with diabetic nephropathy
• Patient education
⚬ Inspect feet daily, never go barefoot; report new wounds, redness, swelling, or drainage immediately
⚬ Maintain long-term glucose control

PATIENT & FAMILY EDUCATION
• Medication Adherence: Complete prescribed antibiotics; understand dosages, schedules, side effects, and 
lab monitoring.
• IV Antibiotic Care: Demonstrate safe administration, aseptic technique, equipment maintenance, and 
proper storage.
• Wound Care: Perform proper dressing changes and monitor for redness, swelling, drainage, or tenderness.
• Infection Prevention: Report fever, chills, rapid pulse, malaise, or worsening wound symptoms immediately.
• Activity & Mobility: Follow weight-bearing restrictions, safely use assistive devices, and avoid pressure on 
graft sites.
• Nutrition & Lifestyle: Maintain a healthy diet, stop smoking, manage weight, and reduce stress to promote 
healing.
• Pain Management: Use prescribed medications and nonpharmacologic pain relief techniques.
• Follow-Up Care: Attend scheduled appointments and lab tests; know when to contact the provider.
• Nursing Priority: Use teach-back method to confirm patient and caregiver understanding.

DISCHARGE PLANNING & HOMECARE
Discharge Planning 
• Antibiotic therapy: Educate the patient on the importance of completing the 
prescribed antibiotic regimen, which may last 6–12 weeks.
• Outpatient IV antibiotic therapy: Some patients may be discharged with a PICC 
line and return for outpatient IV antibiotics or receive them at home with home 
health services. Teach the patient and caregiver proper PICC line care and signs of 
infection.
• Follow-up appointments: Emphasize the importance of attending all scheduled 
provider appointments and laboratory testing to monitor treatment effectiveness.
• Patient and caregiver education: Ensure the patient and family understand the 
treatment plan, wound care procedures, medication administration, and signs of 
complications.
• Nutrition: Encourage a healthy diet rich in protein and vitamins to support bone 
healing and wound recovery.
Home Care
• Wound care: Teach proper dressing 
changes using aseptic technique to prevent 
contamination and promote healing.
• Monitor for infection: Report redness, 
swelling, warmth, tenderness, pus-like 
drainage, fever, chills, rapid pulse, or 
worsening pain to the healthcare provider 
promptly.
• Home health services: Arrange for a home 
health nurse when needed to assist with IV 
antibiotic administration, wound care, and 
monitoring for complications.
• Protect the affected bone: Follow activity 
and weight-bearing restrictions and avoid 
unnecessary pressure on surgical graft 
sites.

A. Shave the surgical site the morning of surgery to reduce bacteria on the skin.
Incorrect:  Shaving the surgical site is no longer performed due to risk for microabrasions that can allow bacteria to enter and cause 
infection. If hair must be removed, clippers are used.
NCLEX QUESTION #1 RATIONALES
B. Elective orthopedic surgery should be postponed if the client has an active infection.
Correct: A patient with an active infection should postpone elective orthopedic surgery, as an existing infection can spread through the 
blood to the surgical site and cause osteomyelitis.
C. The client will be prescribed oral antibiotics for 7-10 days after discharge.
Incorrect: Due to decreased penetration by medications, bone infections are more difficult to treat than soft tissue infections. Therefore, 
osteomyelitis is treated with a longer duration of antibiotic therapy, typically 6-12 weeks and often given through a PICC line.
D. The client should begin full weight-bearing on the affected extremity as soon as possible to promote bone healing and prevent muscle 
atrophy.
Incorrect: Treatment regimens for osteomyelitis restrict weight-bearing activity and encourage immobolization of the affected 
extremity because the infective process weakess the bone and increases the risk for fractures.
E. Obtain blood cultures before initiating antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis treatment.
 Correct: Blood cultures must be obtained before initiating antibiotic therapy to ensure that antibiotics don’t interfere with the 
identification of the infectious organism.

History and Physical
Day 1, 0900:
A 64-year-old client with type 2 diabetes mellitus and peripheral neuropathy is brought to the emergency 
department by their partner. The client reports throbbing left foot pain of 8/10 that worsens with movement, along 
with general malaise for the past several days. The partner states the client has had a “sore on the bottom of the 
foot” for about 8 weeks that “never seems to heal,” and that the client was treated for an infection in the same foot 4 
months ago. A 3 cm x 3cm ulcer is present on the plantar surface of the left first metatarsal head, with a sinus tract 
draining purulent fluid.
NCLEX QUESTION #2
Vital signs
Day 1, 0900:
Temperature: 37.9°C (100.2°F)
Heart rate: 88/min
Respiratory rate: 18/min
Blood pressure: 118/74 mm Hg
SpO2: 96% on room air
Laboratory Results
Day 1, 0945:
Sodium: 143 mEq/L (136 to 145 mEq/L)
Hgb: 9 g/dL (12 to 16 g/dL)
Hct: 27% (37 to 47%)
WBC: 15,800/mm³ (5,000 to 10,000/mm³)
ESR: 16 mm/hr (less than 20 mm/hr)

A. Throbbing left foot pain of 8/10 that worsens with movement
Incorrect: While it can occur with chronic osteomyelitis, throbbing pain is more characteristic of acute osteomyelitis as inflammation and 
pus increases pressure within the bone. In chronic osteomyelitis, inflammation is less severe and drainage relieves pressure, so pain is 
typically dull and persistent, rather than throbbing.
B. The client has had a “sore on the bottom of the foot” for about 8 weeks that “never seems to heal"
Correct: Osteomyelitis is considered chronic when infection lasts for months to years. Acute osteomyelitis develops over days to a few 
weeks and does not involve long-standing nonhealing ulcers.
C. The client was treated for an infection in the same foot 4 months ago
Correct: Recurrence of infection at the same site after treatment is a hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis.
D. Sinus tract draining purulent fluid
Correct: A sinus tract is a channel that forms as pus gradually tunnels from the infected bone to the skin surface. Sinus tracts take time to 
develop, thus this is more characteristic of chronic osteomyelitis rather than acute.
E. Hgb: 9 g/dL (12 to 16 g/dL)
Correct: Long-standing infection can lead to anemia of chronic disease, in which ongoing inflammatory chemicals interfere with RBC production 
and block iron absorption. Anemia is associated with chronic rather than acute osteomyelitis.
F. WBC: 15,800/mm³ (5,000 to 10,000/mm³)
Incorrect: Leukocytosis is more characteristic of acute osteomyelitis, in which the body mounts a sudden immune response. WBC may be normal 
in chronic osteomyelitis, due to the body’s immune response becoming less intense over time.
G. ESR: 16 mm/hr (less than 20 mm/hr)
Correct: ESR is elevated in acute osteomyelitis because of active inflammation, but it may be normal in chronic osteomyelitis as the inflammatory 
response becomes less intense. A normal ESR in a client with signs of bone infection supports a chronic process.
NCLEX QUESTION #2 RATIONALES
